title: Trivial Accessors Without Meaningful Encapsulation
pattern: Private fields are exposed through unvalidated one-to-one getter/setter pairs that add no behavior or useful abstraction, either for a single field or across an entire struct.
why_bad: Accessors add interface ceremony while still exposing the representation: if any value is valid, public fields are simpler and more idiomatic than Java-style boilerplate. When callers coordinate internal state through wholesale accessors, the `private` keyword provides little actual information hiding, the abstraction is shallow, and representation changes (e.g., `timeout_ms` to a `Duration`) ripple outward to every caller.
detection: Pair case: a public getter that merely returns a copy/reference of a field paired with a setter that merely assigns the incoming value. Whole-struct case: every single private field has a matching public getter and setter with no guard condition, calculation, invariant enforcement, or meaningful internal business behavior. Evaluate whether callers are manipulating a deliberate plain data record or coordinating state the object should own.
counterexample: Setters that validate invariants (e.g., checking an age is within range); getters returning computed or cached values; read-only getters for immutable configuration properties; and shared-library interfaces deliberately insulating a stable ABI or compatibility contract from field layout changes.
source: Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 24 ("Refactoring - Class Implementation Refactorings"), p. 187; Fowler, *Refactoring*, Chapter 3.; John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design*, Chapter 5.1 / 5.8 "Information Hiding (and Leakage)" (p. 31, 36).; *John K. Ousterhout - A Philosophy of Software Design (2018)*, Chapter 4, "Modules Should Be Deep" (Shallow Modules, p. 25 & Classitis, p. 26).
